summary: Brick tower lit in 1876 at the Charleston harbor entrance, the third light on Morris Island; closed in 1962, it now stands in open water.

lens.note: Removed when the light was automated in 1938, per LighthouseFriends (which also says a metal frame from the lens is at Hunting Island Lighthouse).

access.note: Tower closed; grounds open. State-owned, leased to Save The Light, Inc.

facts.agency: State of South Carolina (owner, Department of Natural Resources); Save The Light, Inc. (lessee)

events.note: Colonial tower built on Middle Bay Island (first lighthouse on the site)
South Carolina hands the light and island to the federal government
Second tower with a revolving light, per the nomination only; the Charleston history site says the sources do not settle whether a new tower was built in 1837 or 1857.
Second-order Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends and Charleston history site); the nomination describes a first-order lens in the 1876 tower

Antebellum tower blown up by Confederate forces, night of 18-19 December 1861 (Charleston history site); LighthouseFriends gives 25 December 1861 and calls the tower the island's first lighthouse. The sources disagree on which tower it was.
Present brick tower completed, built on the site of the 1767 tower
Lard oil replaced by mineral oil (nomination)
Cyclone of 25 August 1885 knocked down part of the wall around the tower and dwelling
August 1886 earthquake jarred the lens out of place and cracked the tower in two places
Fuel changed to acetylene (nomination); LighthouseFriends dates the automatic acetylene light to 1938
Keepers and families leave the island
Discontinued when the Sullivan's Island light went into service on 15 June 1962
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP 82003837)
Save The Light, Inc. buys the tower for $75,000
State of South Carolina accepts title; Save The Light signs a 99-year lease

notes_for_editor: Height: the 1982 nomination gives a 150-foot tower; the record's 49 m (161 ft) is not confirmed by any source read, so the story gives no record height. Lens order in 1858: second-order per LighthouseFriends and the Charleston history site (which also reports the Coast Guard entry as first-order); first-order per the nomination for the 1876 tower. The 1876 light's character: the nomination says revolving; the Board's 1876 report and notice say fixed white (Charleston history site). Fuel: the nomination dates mineral oil to 1881 and acetylene to 1934; LighthouseFriends dates mineral oil to 1884 and the automatic acetylene light to 22 June 1938. Jetties: the nomination dates them to 1896 and blames them for erosion; the Charleston history site dates construction 1878-1895 and says the shore was retreating earlier. The story reports both. Towers before 1876: the nomination gives a second tower in 1837; the Charleston history site says the sources do not settle 1837 or 1857. Which tower was blown up in 1861: the Charleston history site calls it the antebellum tower; LighthouseFriends calls it the island's first lighthouse and dates it 25 December 1861. The story uses the antebellum wording and states the disagreement. The 1876 tower and the 1767 beacon: the nomination says directly on top; the Charleston history site disputes it. Keepers' houses: the nomination describes three frame Italianate residences; LighthouseFriends describes a three-story dwelling (the story does not give a count). Keeper dates: the Save The Light list gives John Wieking 1885-1908 against the archive's 1885-1912; the story uses the archive. The Save The Light list also says Lighthouse Service records after 1908 were lost in a fire; the archive roster is built from NARA registers and runs to 1938. Roster count: 90 stints (roster.py). Position: the USLHS place record puts the place at 32.7583, -79.8433, about 7 km northeast of the record position (32.6954, -79.8836), which matches the nomination's setting and the Wikipedia coordinates. The record position is kept. Owners and buyers: LighthouseFriends names the 1965 buyer (John Preston Richardson, $3,303.03), the 1966 buyer (St. Elmo Felkel, $25,000) and the 1996 foreclosure buyer (Paul Gunter); the story leaves them unnamed and uses Save The Light's dates. Name matches not linked: Haig Point's Richard Stonebridge and Charles L. Sisson appear on this roster too (see the Haig Point notes); the archive gives both the same person slugs. Unverified: the 1885 cyclone and 1886 earthquake come from the Charleston history site, which cites the Coast Guard Historian's Office; the Coast Guard page was not reachable in the archive copies tried. Wikipedia cites Light-House Board reports for the 1873-1876 appropriations and the 1885 cyclone; those reports are not in the local corpus (it starts in 1891), so the story leaves those figures out. The 1884 Life-Saving Service proposal for a Morris Island station has no station record here. Names matched by column position: none.
